title: The fox and the moon
summary: A little fox goes out at night for the very first time, sees the moon and decides to bring it down. It won't be caught, but he finds something better.

scenes.text:
That night, for the very first time, the little fox came out of the den.

Before letting him go, his mother licked his ear.

"Stay near the entrance," she said. "Where I can see you."

The little fox put out one paw. Then the other. Then his whole nose. The forest smelled of cold earth and wet leaves, and at night everything looked bigger than in the daytime.

Then he looked up.

Among the branches there was something round, white and still, like an enormous biscuit someone had left behind in the tree.

"Mama," he asked quietly, "what's that?"

"That's the moon."

The little fox could not take his eyes off it. It was the most beautiful thing he had ever seen. And if it was up there, caught in the branches, maybe it could be brought down.

His mother turned to sniff at a root, and the little fox ran off.

He ran between the trees. He hopped over a fallen log. He crossed a clearing where the grass was so tall it tickled his tummy. The moon was always ahead of him, just a little further on.

"It's on the hill," he told himself. "I bet it's resting on the hill."

He climbed the hill with his tongue hanging out. At the top there was nobody. The moon was still up in the sky, just as far away as before, as if it hadn't noticed the race at all.

The little fox took a run-up, stretched his front paws as far as they would go, and made a leap.

He landed on his back in the grass.

He stayed like that for a long while, looking up at it. His tail hurt a little, and his pride hurt a lot.

He went down the other side of the hill, slowly, dragging his tail.

At the bottom there was a big puddle, so still it looked like a mirror lying on the ground. The little fox was about to walk around it when he stopped dead.

The moon was there.

Inside the water. Right in front of his paws.

"Found you," he said, very softly, so as not to frighten it.

He crept closer, hardly breathing. He reached out a paw and touched it.

The moon broke into a hundred little pieces of silver that trembled on the water.

The little fox sprang backwards. But the pieces calmed down, joined together again, and the moon was whole once more, looking at him as if nothing had happened.

And the little fox burst out laughing.

When he got back, his mother was waiting at the entrance of the den, her ears standing straight up.

"Where were you?"

The little fox didn't know where to begin. That he had climbed a hill. That he had jumped with all his might. That he had put his paw right on the moon, and the moon had broken, and then it had mended itself.

"I went to fetch the moon," he said at last. "But it won't let itself be caught."

His mother looked up, and so did he.

There it was, right above the den tree. It had followed him all the way home.

"That's because it isn't for catching," said his mother. "It's for keeping you company."

The little fox curled up against her warm tummy. Before he closed his eyes he looked once more, to make sure it was still there.

It was. And like that, in good company, he fell asleep.
